title: How a Muddy Hole Becomes a Water Well
script: If you're dying of thirst and you dig a hole until mud starts to seep in, you have a water well. But the dirt walls cave in and nearly bury you, so you start again and line the hole with a ring of stones as you dig. This is a well lining. But every rainstorm washes dirt and dung straight into your water, so you build a wall around the top and a sloped apron that sheds dirty water away. In 1854, a London well dug three feet from a leaking cesspit spread cholera and killed hundreds, and that is why wells sit far from toilets. But pulling up a heavy bucket by hand wrecks your back, so you wind the rope around a log with a crank. This is a windlass. But then a dry summer drops the water table below the bottom of your well, so you dig deeper, down into the wet layer of rock and sand. This is an aquifer, not an underground lake, just rock and sand soaked with water like a sponge. But now it's too deep to haul by hand, so you add a hand pump. But air pressure can only lift water about ten meters, and you're deeper than that, so you lower an electric pump into the water, and it pushes instead of pulls. Add a sealed cap, a pressure tank, and a pipe to your kitchen. Congratulations, you have built a water well.
